calls.head: Like for like: Sasson vs. Nesterenko
calls.body: At home, the Canucks keep sending Sasson’s line (Cotter, Sasson and Gallagher) out against opponents’ fourth lines, far more often than chance would suggest. Manny Malhotra keeps choosing line for line. Tonight the Ducks’ fourth line is Malott, McQueen and Nesterenko.
calls.call: The Canucks’ L4 (Cotter, Sasson and Gallagher) spends at least 38% of its 5-on-5 time against the Ducks’ fourth line, against about 25% with no line matching.
calls.nums: At home: 50% of this group’s 5-on-5 time against fourth lines, about 25% with no line matching

With no line matching, this group would face fourth lines about 25% of the time, about as often as those lines are on the ice.

calls.happened: Vancouver’s L4 (Cotter, Sasson, Gallagher) spent 31% of its 5-on-5 time against Anaheim’s L4 (2:35 of 8:20). The call needed 38%, halfway from the 25% it would get with no line matching to its home habit of 50%.

lane.tip: Share of this group’s 5-on-5 time against that line tonight (the filled dot). The ring is the call: halfway from what it would get with no line matching (the tick) to its home habit (the dotted mark), since part of any habit is luck. Reaching the ring holds the call; past the tick is partly; otherwise it didn’t happen.

calls.title: Cotter, Sasson and Gallagher saw the Ducks’ fourth line some of the time
calls.plain: Vancouver sent Cotter, Sasson and Gallagher out against the Ducks’ fourth line more than they would with no line matching, but not as often as the call needed.
calls.said: Manny Malhotra would send Cotter, Sasson and Gallagher out against the Ducks’ fourth line again

calls.head: The Ducks’ edge in the penalty kill
calls.body: The Ducks are around the middle of the league for the penalty kill, and the Canucks are the worst. It’s the widest gap between these two, though not a huge one. Anaheim’s penalty kill has been near the bottom of the league for years, though.
calls.call: The Ducks’ penalty kill allows less per 60 than the Canucks’.

calls.happened: On expected goals allowed per 60 on the penalty kill, Anaheim had 6.7 per 60 and Vancouver 14.9 per 60. Coming in, Anaheim was at 7.5 per 60 and Vancouver at 9.0 per 60.

calls.title: Anaheim’s kill gave up less
calls.plain: The Ducks came out clearly ahead on the penalty kill, as the gap between these two suggested. On the scoreboard, Anaheim killed 3 of 5 penalties and Vancouver 0 of 3.
calls.said: the Ducks’ penalty kill would give up less than the Canucks’
calls.beyond: Vancouver has one of the league’s leakiest penalty kills. Even by those standards, this was a big night: 3 power-play goals on 3 chances. A power play like theirs against a kill like Vancouver’s scores 3 or more about once every 45 games.

VAN.head: We gave Vancouver only a 38% chance, and it went the way we feared.

ANA.head: We gave Anaheim a 62% chance, and they delivered.

surprises.head: Anaheim couldn’t get good looks
surprises.body: Vancouver usually gives up some of the league’s most dangerous shots. Not tonight: Anaheim’s shots at 5-on-5 had a 4.3% chance of scoring on the average shot, against their usual 6.2% (about 6.7% against Vancouver) and a league average of 6.3%. A team strays this far about once every 50 games.

surprises.head: A rough night for Kevin Lankinen
surprises.body: Lankinen allowed 5 goals on 22 shots, worth 2.1 expected goals: 2.9 more than expected. Starting goalies have a night this rough about once every 30 starts.

story.head: Gauthier bags a hat trick
paras: Early in the first, Mikael Granlund opened the scoring for the Ducks on the power play, and Jacob Quillan and Roger McQueen fought. Liam Öhgren tied it 1-1 for Vancouver on the power play early in the first. Cutter Gauthier put the Ducks ahead for good on the power play late in the period, and Leo Carlsson made it 3-1 shorthanded early in the second. Travis Mitchell and Quillan dropped the gloves early in the period. Midway through the second, Linus Karlsson cut Anaheim’s lead to 3-2, and Jamie Oleksiak and Jeff Malott squared off. Gauthier struck again on the power play late in the second to make it 4-2 for the Ducks. Gauthier completed his hat trick early in the third to make it 5-2, and that one stood up as the winner. Two fights broke out at once early in the period, and Max Sasson, Sam Colangelo, Noah Warren and Paul Cotter all got five for fighting. Jake DeBrusk scored later in the period and again just over four minutes later to make it 5-4, but the Ducks held on. It was his second straight hat trick. Beckett Sennecke assisted on all three, and had four assists in all. Granlund finished with a goal and two assists.

Nothing much separated these two on the chances. This one could have gone either way. Laurent Brossoit, in his second game since coming over from San Jose, made 19 saves for the Ducks, and Kevin Lankinen allowed five goals on 22 shots.

The Ducks went 3-for-3 on the power play. Colangelo and Cotter were both thrown out of the game. The Ducks moved to 7-7-1 and climbed to fourth in the Pacific, while the Canucks fell to 3-13-1, still last in the NHL.
